extracted.intended_audience: poets, artists, philosophers, and students of aesthetics / literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging poetic/aesthetic value: how poetry should treat morality, truth, movement (grace), and beauty (architectonic vs accidental), and what kinds of subjects and representations produce aesthetic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of aesthetic and moral judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: An object has less aesthetic value the more it bears the character of a moral object; the poet should avoid calling attention to the moral law and instead appeal to the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets should not subordinate aesthetic aims to moral didacticism. Bringing reason's rule to the foreground undermines the imagination's necessary independence; if treating moral subjects, present the power of the will imaginatively rather than appeal to duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic end: rejoice the soul and elevate the spiritual faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's proper end is to rejoice the soul by contemplative spectacle; aesthetic pleasure comes from what improves personality and elevates spiritual faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should aim at enlarging the reader's spiritual feeling rather than instructing them in particular moral acts. Only what heightens spiritual force brings authentic aesthetic joy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic interest in the possibility of free will
rubrics_metrics.description: The aesthetic charm of moral action arises from the idea of the possibility of an absolutely free will, not from proof that duty has been actually performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentations that make the possibility of freedom salient (showing faculty of choice or force of will) are aesthetically effective because they allow the imagination to feel its own freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth = possibility, not historic truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic truth consists in what may have happened (possibility), not in whether it historically occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic impressions rest on poetic truth. Historic reality can be an incidental addition but is not constitutive of poetic effect. Fictions that are possible often produce equal or greater poetic force than strictly historical accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on national/historical subject-matter as artistic crutch
rubrics_metrics.description: Using national events or conforming invention to real history to gain effect is an accidental stimulant and not proper to poetic art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not convert poetry into a memorializing of national themes or let memory/learning become the interpreter; poetry should go straight to the heart and aim at the human being, not the citizen. National themes are often a borrowed force for writers lacking form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's indirect moral influence rather than direct instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is ill-suited as an instrument for carrying out particular projects or direct moral instruction; it affects character indirectly by forming dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use poetry to shape general character and inspire greatness (like love forming a hero) rather than as a tool for explicit counsel, propaganda, or practical tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize depiction of force and freedom over moral direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic judgment attends more to the force and freedom of the will than to its moral direction; freedom and strength increase aesthetic interest even at cost of moral regularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrayals that display energy, freedom, and resolute will (even in evil acts) are often more aesthetically compelling than portrayals of purely dutiful virtue. Example: Medea's vengeance becomes sublime because it involves sacrifice and force of will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic value of intense (even vicious) characters with potential for change
rubrics_metrics.description: Vices that manifest great force of will can arouse aesthetic interest because they reveal aptitude for moral liberty and the possibility of transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters with intense, decisive wills (even wicked ones) are interesting because a single act of will might convert their force to virtue; by contrast, middling characters who show no possibility of absolute liberty are less compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace as movable/accidental beauty (beauty of movement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grace is a movable beauty — an accidental property separable from the subject — and corresponds to beauty of movement which can be added to an otherwise less-beautiful subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent grace as a changeable, objective feature arising in movement (not mere impression from dress). The myth of the girdle symbolizes a property that can be conferred and is manifest in movement rather than static form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace limited to human voluntary movements expressing moral sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Grace belongs exclusively to human voluntary movements that express the moral order; it does not extend to mere sensuous or purely animal/physical movements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking to evoke grace, focus on voluntary acts that show inner moral feeling. Avoid attributing grace to purely physical phenomena (e.g., waves, branches) or to movements grounded solely in appetite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish architectonic (fixed) beauty from grace (accidental beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectonic beauty (beauty of structure) is the fixed beauty determined by nature's necessity — proportion, form, tone — distinct from accidental grace produced by mind or movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate physical/structural beauty on senses' immediate perception (proportions, form) separate from accidental features caused by will. Do not conflate technical perfection or moral dignity with pure sensuous beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as sensory phenomenon that can also please the understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty originates in the world of sense and is judged immediately by the senses, but the understanding can adopt sensible phenomena by associating its own ideas with them, letting beauty also please the intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create works whose sensible appearance naturally invites the understanding to associate suitable ideas (symbols). There must be a fitting relation between phenomenon and the idea the understanding brings in; taste mediates between sense and intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form should justify its beauty without recourse to intellectual concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: To be judged beautiful by the senses, a human form should justify its superiority on immediate appearance alone; appealing to moral dignity or intelligence to increase apparent beauty converts the judgment into an intellectual one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting imagery or characterization aimed at aesthetic appreciation, ensure the sensory qualities themselves suffice for beauty rather than relying on explanatory intellectual or moral backstory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty derived from free arbitrariness in human action
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifications arising from free will (accidents due to mind) contribute to a part of beauty that nature did not strictly determine; this accidental beauty differs from nature's fixed architectonic beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict actions and movements that originate in freedom as sources of aesthetic interest distinct from purely natural form. Recognize that nature bears responsibility for fixed beauty but not for beauty introduced by free choice.
